title: Why Do Geese Fly in a V? 🪿
description:
Why do geese fly in a V? Each bird rides the rising air that curls off the wingtip of the bird ahead, which saves energy: pelicans flying in formation had heart rates up to 14% lower, and ibises take turns in the tiring front spot.

Sources:
https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/birds-that-fly-in-a-v-formation-use-an-amazing-trick
https://www.ox.ac.uk/node/29050

topic: Why do geese fly in a V?
script:
Birds in a V can cut their heart rate 14 percent,
and you've never seen why.
It's the secret behind every V of geese.
Each flap pushes air down behind the wing.
But at the wingtip, air curls up and around,
into a spinning swirl.
Just outside that swirl, the air is rising.
So the bird behind slides into that exact spot,
and gets free lift on every flap.
Line everyone up like that,
and you get a V.
Pelicans tracked in formation
had heart rates up to 14 percent lower than flying solo.
Ibises even time their flaps to match the bird ahead.
But the front bird gets no free ride.
So ibises take turns,
swapping the tiring spot at the front.
Honestly, that's teamwork with zero meetings.
So which bird would you rather be,
the leader at the front, or the one in the back?
key_facts: Wingtip vortices create rising air (upwash) just outside each wingtip; a following bird placed there gets extra lift (Portugal et al. 2014, Nature, via National Geographic)
Great white pelicans flying in formation had heart rates 11-14% lower than flying alone (Weimerskirch et al. 2001, Nature)
Northern bald ibises time their wingbeats to match the upwash of the bird ahead (Portugal et al. 2014)
Ibises in V formation take turns leading, swapping the costly front position (Voelkl et al. 2015, PNAS, via Oxford)
